summary: The day lends itself to three Python tasks on rules a function can show, keeping a sum at the fact's grain, picking the type 2 version in force on a date and overwriting a dimension as a type 1 on copies; its modeling levels, star and snowflake queries and BigQuery physical design are concepts, BigQuery-only SQL or the demo's own rungs.

steps.title: Data models: from business questions to tables
steps.reason: The step teaches a concept: a model is the agreed plan, and each "by" in a business question names a dimension. Nothing in it returns a value a check can read.

steps.title: Conceptual, logical and physical models
steps.reason: The three levels are a way of describing a design, and the one table a function could hold (MySQL types against BigQuery types) is a lookup whose only wrong answer is a mistyped entry, not a mistake the page names.

steps.title: Dimensional modeling: facts, dimensions, measures and grain
steps.reason: The page's own loop shows the grain mistake as a wrong number: a ticket-level value summed over every event row gives 26 where 13 is right. A function over event-row tuples, which the page unpacks in a for loop, returns that number, and both checks are failed by summing or counting every row instead of the closing events.

steps.title: The star schema built for the desk
steps.reason: Its checkable pieces (the YYYYMMDD date key, agent key 0, the WHERE lines that drop bad events) are rungs the 03-star-schema demo types into star.sql, and GENERATE_DATE_ARRAY and QUALIFY do not run on the page's SQLite 3.39.0. A plain star query on sqlite3 has no wrong answer the page names beyond not writing it, and the demo's questions.sql already takes the per-agent and per-weekday queries.

steps.title: The snowflake schema and when its joins pay
steps.reason: The page's point is that the star and snowflake forms return the same rows and differ in joins and repeated text, a design trade-off; a snowflake query on sqlite3 would only be wrong by not being written, and nested, repeated fields are BigQuery-only.

steps.title: The physical model in BigQuery: partitions, clusters and the cache
steps.reason: Partitioning, clustering, the query cache, the dry run and the sandbox's 60-day expiry are BigQuery features and costs, reached through bq or a project; the runtime has no BigQuery and a check cannot see bytes billed.

steps.title: Slowly changing dimensions: types 0 to 6 and how to choose
steps.reason: The effective-date rule (from inclusive, to exclusive) is the same comparison in Python on date objects, which the next step says compare with < and >=. A lookup of the version in force on a day is failed by the three mistakes the page and brief name: reading is_current, matching on the customer id alone, and treating effective_to as inclusive.

steps.title: SCD type 2 in Python, tested
steps.reason: The pure-function shape the page teaches (copy the rows with a list comprehension, map ids with a dict comprehension, next key from max with default=0) shows up as returned rows and an untouched input. apply_scd2 is the 04-customer-history demo rung, so the task is its type 1 sibling from the previous step's table; pytest, the BigQuery load and CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS stay out.

tasks.title: Facts and grain
tasks.idea: The reader writes close_summary(rows), where each row is an event tuple (kind, ticket_id, hours_since_open) at the fact's grain, and returns a tuple (tickets_closed, total_hours) taken from the closing events only. For [("open", 1, 0), ("assigned", 1, 1), ("closed", 1, 3), ("open", 3, 0), ("closed", 3, 10), ("open", 4, 0)] it returns (2, 13).
checks: total_hours is 13 for the example rows; summing hours_since_open over every event row adds the assignment's hour and mixes the grain.
tickets_closed is 2; counting every row, or every row of a ticket that has a closing event, counts each ticket more than once.
A ticket with only open and assigned events, such as ticket 4, adds to neither number.

tasks.title: Slowly changing dimensions
tasks.idea: The reader writes fee_on(dimension, customer_id, day), where dimension is a list of type 2 customer rows as dicts with customer_id, monthly_fee, effective_from, effective_to and is_current (dates as date objects), and returns the monthly_fee of the version in force on day: effective_from <= day < effective_to. With Dana's two rows (49.00 from 2026-10-01 to 2026-11-05, 199.00 from 2026-11-05 to 9999-12-31) and another customer's row, fee_on(rows, 1, date(2026, 10, 20)) returns Decimal("49.00").
checks: An October day returns 49.00; returning the row whose is_current is True gives 199.00, the overwrite the page warns about.
The change day 2026-11-05 returns 199.00; treating effective_to as inclusive with <= picks the closed 49.00 row.
A day in late November returns 199.00 when the closed row comes first in the list; matching on customer_id alone returns the first version found.

tasks.title: SCD in Python
tasks.idea: The reader writes apply_scd1(dimension, source), the type 1 sibling of the page's apply_scd2: it returns new rows in which each source customer's row has name, email, country and monthly_fee overwritten under its existing customer_key, and a customer not yet in the dimension is appended with the next surrogate key. Given Dana at key 1 and fee 49.00 and a source row with fee 199.00, it returns one row, key 1, fee 199.00.
checks: A changed customer keeps one row under its old customer_key with the new fee; adding a second row is type 2, not type 1.
The dimension passed in is left as it was; writing into its dicts instead of copies changes the caller's rows.
A new customer gets the next key after the highest one, and an empty dimension starts at key 1; max without default=0 raises on an empty dimension.
